blocks.x: Well, I think, you know, Mike Casimir sent us a take with you before, so we've got a lot of the stuff down. I just want to follow up on it. Maybe the first thing we can get is your full name.

Well, my name is Albert Nicholas. You don't have any middle name on it. No, I had a middle name. I dropped it. My name was Albert Joseph Nicholas when I was christened. I dropped it. It's for Albert Nicholas, Jr. Let's get everybody else's name. Okay, Hans, let's go.

And I'm Dick Allen, and Lars Edergren is coming later. He's busy eating breakfast. Let's see, today is June the 20th, what's the date? 26th. 26th, 1972, and we're at 931 Charlotte Street, Lars Edergren's apartment. Oh, one of the things that, you remember Alan Ward, who's a friend of Mike Casimir, he was telling me that you took lessons from Tio? That's right, Lorenzo Tio. Who else would be there at the lessons at the same time? Did you meet any other musicians?
Yeah, yeah. Jimmy Noon was ahead of me. I was second, and Barney Begard and Omar Simeon. Omar Simeon, he was in Chicago. And those were, we were the four major students of Tio.
Mm-hmm.
Old man Tio and his son Lorenzo.
What about somebody like Johnny Dodge? Did you ever see him there?

Oh, yes. I knew Johnny Dodge all through the years. When I was 12, 13 years old, I used to hear him at Uptown at Miss Cores along with Ory's, the kid Ory and things like that. I was a kid, but I always admired his playing. I don't think he'd take any lessons with any teachers down time. He had a unique style of his own. He was very popular. Yeah. Liked him very much.
Was he your age? No, he's older than me.
Johnny's about four years older than me. I saw his son two years ago when I came to New Orleans driving a taxi. That was really funny.
Rudy, yeah.

Yeah, it looks just like Johnny. My son and I, we got in the taxi and we were talking about, this was around six o'clock at night, we were walking around. We had our car parked on Durban here in Ironville. We were talking about how things have changed through the years. Then he turned around and asked my son, he said, are you a musician? My son said, no, not me, but my dad is. He said, well, my dad was also. I said, who was your dad? He said, Johnny Dodge. I said, what? He said, do you know him? I said, man, I should say I do. So he said, well, who are you? I said, I'm Albert Nicklin. He said, what? He said, he had my pictures when I was young, you know, in Chicago. He was a kid. So that brought on a session.
Oh, yeah.

And he's a very nice guy. And then we had to stop and he said, man, I have a brother. And she called, well, you know, Sharon's been listening. And he got there, gave him a buzz and told me he met me. And he's a very pleasant guy. I didn't see him this time yet. I haven't seen him. I haven't seen him either. But a very nice guy. He's very sharp.
Well, what about Johnny? How did he get interested in music? Do you know? Was he interested? Who? Johnny Dodge. Did you know him when he got interested?

No, when I met Johnny, he was playing. He was playing his head off around 1912. At Betsy Cole. No, Ms. Cole's Lauren. I don't know. We used to say Ms. Cole's Lauren. It used to be penny parties on Sundays, you know, for the youngsters, you know. I was a kid, twelve years old, and I used to go up there. And I was learning time and time, and he was respiring quite a bit. And Johnny was up. And then, of course, I met him to the years. She called. I took his place. And King Howard was playing in 24. When they left the band, he wasn't playing sax. And I was playing sax, and so King sent for Bonnie and myself, Paul, Bob, Rimmie, and Wistler. And I got to know him real well.
Mm-hmm. Did the... When you first joined Oliver, who was the trombone player? George Fields. George Fields. George Fields.
Yeah, old George Fields. He was dead, I think. Mm-hmm. Then we sent and got Ori in California. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
What did Ori play then? He played trombone.
Yeah. He sent and got him and came to Chicago.
Did he play any other instruments?
No.
Did you ever hear him play sax or anything?
No, no, no, no. Just... Yeah. I think he would play a little bass, too, on the side. You know, this one.
Yeah, he plays different instruments. Yeah, yeah. I just wondered if he ever doubled, you know.
No, no, no. He didn't double.
So many guys doubled. No. What about people like Zoo Robertson? Were they around there?
Zoo? He actually was an old time, around 24. Yeah, Zoo is in New Orleans. And we went to Chicago.
That's the... Louie was up there already. He left a year ahead of me. Uh-huh.

He was supposed to play at the Royal Garden and burn down. And we waited and went into the plantation profane. It was a beautiful place. Uh-huh. Then they hold a band there. What was it like then? Was there much burning and explosions and all that? No, those were the gangsters. I remember one night in our club, somebody planted a bomb on the roof.
And it went off exactly 12 o'clock at night, just before the review came on.

In those days you had to play review at 12 o'clock. And man, this day one of the big things. And I was like, I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. But this day one of the rituals had to build their bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo And all the drapers were coming down, you could look up and see the moon. And you think the people would run? They sat on there and the cops come in and say, you all have to get out. And they were ordering drinks and just like nothing happened. And the band Joe said, come on, we gotta play, you know. And the cops said, you better plug it off that stand because there might be another bomb, you might be under the stand in case the bathroom didn't go off another. So then the guys grab the horns and don't split them. I remember it very well in the summertime.
Do you remember Half Plane Jackson, Frankie Jackson? Singer and entertainer, you know?
I think your name is familiar. Maybe I do. A little short, then. Half Plane, I think I remember. It's a long time ago.
I just wondered who was in those reviews.

Now the names got away from...let's see. Oh yeah, Dickie Wells and Jimmy and Dickie, they were two dancers. They were young. And who else? You had a girl, she came to New York later on. She was a very good singer and dancer, although she used to do a split, and split all across the slope. I've forgotten her name. She was gonna sing a little bit. And who else? Oh. There was a blues singer, a big one like...she was from St. Louis, Missouri. She had a hell of a voice, a big sound like the first blues singer. What's her name? The first one.
When I think of Ma Rainey and Bessie Smith.
Bessie Smith. She was like Bessie. She was big like Bessie. And she had the same sound. She sang some beautiful blues also. Around 24 and 25. Forget her name. So you had lots of acts along with them.
Oh yeah.

You had a review of what, ten girls dancing. And you had individual artists like singers and tap dancers. You know, things like that. Bill Robinson's dancing now playing songs. You had tumblers. An act that used to tumble. And every two weeks they changed the show. Then another show. But you keep the same chorus. But new stars would come in every week. That was Ada Brown, I think. Ada Brown, that's her. That's her.
The one you recorded with?
No, no. That's the one I'm referring to. Yeah. She was at the plantation. Yeah, that's that. Ada Brown, that's her name.
I think she was James Scott's cousin. You know the guy that wrote Climax Rag and all that.
What? Yeah, but I know she was a big one. She had a sound. She could sing. Ada Brown, that's her. I think she did, man.
She made Panama Limited and all that. She had a sound, man.
We used to push that guy. Oh, yeah. Tell you the problem.
Did you ever work with Tommy Leidener in Chicago?
Yes, yes, yes. Tommy was with us before he went to Europe.
Oh, I'm sorry.

Yeah. It was Tommy and King. See, Lewis left us to go with Fletcher Hennessy in 24. Tommy took his place. Then he went with this man, or I forgot, Sam Wooden. And then after he left, then Bob Shaffler came with me. And he stayed with the man until I left.
Did you work with Louis at the same time with King Arthur? Yes. You were there. Yes, yes. I was in band with Louis. That's it. Did you make many tours? Yes, we toured in Pennsylvania.
We toured for a couple of weeks in South Bend, Indiana. That's right. And Pennsylvania also. We had a couple of, two weeks tour like that. One night. It was very nice. Very good.
Did you have any trouble transferring with the union up there then? No, no.

You see, at that time, the union was just starting. They're begging you to join. They're almost giving you a card. You know, they had no union in Orleans at that time. I see. And I think it was about five or ten dollars to join a union and all that stuff. And we joined right away.
What about Rudy Jackson? Was he around?

That's right. I played with him in the band also. You see, I came before Bonnie and Paul. Joe said for me in 23. I had a band at Tom Anderson on Ramport and Canal. On Ramport and I was there. And Jimmy Noon came down from Mardi Gras. And we had a hell of a band then. And Bonnie, we were just running sax, you know. And Bonnie was playing ten. I was playing alto and clarinet. And Lewis Russell, Paul Bobbin, Willie San Diego. And I know him at Twyre on trumpet. He was a very nice trumpet player. They thought it was Manuel Perez.
Mm-hmm.

But it was I know him at Twyre. Very fine reader. And Jimmy Noon, he came down. He heard his name and said, what? And he went back. When he got back to Chicago, he told Joe, he said, man, Albin, they've got a band. You should hit them, kids. So that's when Joe sent for us, you know. To come. And he sent for me first. I made this tour with him in Pennsylvania, in South Bend, Indiana, for a couple of weeks. Then I came back to New Orleans and got with the band again. Then he decided to send for us for. Oh, I see.
Mm-hmm.
Well, what about Johnny Lindsay? You ever worked with him up there?
That's right. Johnny Lindsay was with us on this tour. Oh. He was playing the trombone.
Mm-hmm. That's right.
Johnny Lindsay was with us, yeah.
Oh. Well, I think I have it straight now. What happened? You went with that one band. Yeah, yeah. Rudy Jackson and Louie.
That's right. Rudy Jackson was in the band. And I took Buster Bailey's place. Buster was playing with Joe before.
Mm-hmm.
And Johnny Dodds, well, they left. And I took that place. And me and Rudy. Yeah, Rudy was playing ten of them.
Who did the arrangements for that first band?

That first album? Oh, I don't know. Let's see. He had, well, mostly, we had stock arrangements and just a little skeleton move. Mm-hmm. Just to keep you together, you know. Mm-hmm. Big Randy like now. Mm-hmm. But he liked his music. Joe was pretty clever. And he liked to hear everybody in the band. No one person, no. He wanted to hear everybody blended. He was a good leader. Oh. And he was sharp. And we had discipline in the band. And sometime we'd be playing a new number for just rehearsing and everybody's going to just a shh. Now let me hear those feet out on the floor.
Mm-hmm.
And you have to, you see, any fool can play loud.
That's the first thing you learn when you play music, all that noise. Mm-hmm.

To play music, you've got a phrase. Mm-hmm. You know, bring your notes up and down. You know, make it music-wise. I noticed that with these jazz bands around here. They still go loud, but maybe because they call them the public, you know, the poems like Danny Ball. You know, they don't get down and phrase, you know. Like Orenham used to do in the old days. Mm-hmm. Buddy Petit had a little band here. Oh, the Friar, when I was a kid coming up and said, you know, I was a kid. I don't ever say, man, I joined. That man was way ahead this time.
Mm-hmm.

Oh, man. You could hear the guitar and bass, and we didn't use the piano. Mm-hmm. And what a band. And Buddy didn't blast. He played full trumpet. And Morris French is on trombone. Oh, man. I'm careful. You guys have always been talking about Morris French. Oh, he was trombone, man. And those guys were great. But now they're making how loud you can play. It's like, you know, it don't make sense. It's good for the public outside, you know, to come in. But music-wise...
You could hear the toilet, man. I'm telling you, man. They play so burned loud.
They were surprised that night. I sat in at the preservation hall. And, well, this cat, he didn't play too loud a trumpet player. Who was it? It was... It was... It was... It was... It was...
It was...

It was... It was... I had a good reed. I played loud, but I don't like to just blow the grains out. Yeah. When it comes up to that point, I'll play loud. It'll soften again, you know. And it's a feeling.
What did they teach you? You reminded me of something. What about vibrato when you were studying under Tio?

Well, I had to study that. That's a different study. I was learning music when I was a Tio. I took lessons two years without the instrument. I was small. I was about nine years old. Then when I got to be eleven, they gave me the clarinet. Well, I knew the clarinet. My uncle was junior, you know.
I used to watch him all the time.

I learned the clarinet. I knew the famous one. And in a week, I was playing my lessons and things. I studied it. And now, the vibrato, that comes in. That's a different study. And you're breathing. That's another thing. That's a different study. You see, I'm talking to you and I can hold my breath.
I'm talking.
I'm not beating anywhere. That's the thing. I don't know how to learn. You know me, huh?
Yeah.

Because if you blow, you get tired. I wouldn't last. That's tiresome. But I'm blowing. I'm talking. I'm talking. I'm talking. I'm talking. It's down here. And I know, consciously. I don't know what happens. I know when to cut my notes to go into the next four bars or something. Because when I'm playing, I'm always thinking at least eight bars ahead. Sure of what I'm doing, I never guess on nobody's job. I don't practice. I practice at home. But when I'm playing, I'm concentrating at least eight bars ahead. Nothing slip upon me. I learned that when I was a kid. Old Papa Teo told me, don't just read your notes and the next one. No, you look ahead. And you play the same way. That's a musician. But we all do that. God. It's tough a while to see if it's real. You want to get some?
I'll try it in there. Okay.
Yeah, we were talking about breathing and vibrato. Things like that. How do you get your vibrato?
It's with the throat and the lips. You concentrate. I don't know, it's something that you practice in. It comes.
You know how to move your jaw.

Yeah, yeah, your jaw and things like that. It's a practice though. Some guys have a bigger one than others. And you got to use different ones. Like if I'm playing with a band, say. I played a little classical also when I was a kid. They use a straight sound. They don't use heavy vibrato. All the band is straight. Jazz, vibrato. And you get with a section. If you're a first alto player, say like in the reed section, the first alto, he keeps the band, the reeds together. But you try to get his vibe brighter so we all can blend. That's very important also.
Did you, well which sax did you play with, say Louis Russell?

I played third alto. I played first alto. Charlie Holmes was on third. And Tenny Hill when I joined the band in 29, was on tenor. Then later on we had two tenors and two altos. I played for about two years alto. Then it changed me to tenor. And I played first tenor when Greely Walton came in the band. I was playing alto when Greely came. Then we marched in the band with four, with four. And Louis came in the band. Then I went on first tenor. I played until 1940. I'd switch up and down. Sometime I'd play alto, sometime I'd play that. Then I played baritone sax also. I played baritone. And all the clarinet worked got just for me in the band. And we had three other trumpets besides Louis. We had Red Island, Otis Johnson, and Hemp Hill, and Louis. It was four trumpets, three trumpets. We had Higginbottom, George Washington, very good trumpets. And the Paris, Sidney the Paris. I know, Wilbur the Paris.
That's not the same George Washington that was down here in New Orleans.
I don't know, he was in New York.
It was a real short little George Washington that used to play with Buddy Petit. No, no, no.

That's another guy. He was a good arranger also. He used to arrange for us in the band. We had a couple of rangers in the band. George Washington was a good arranger. He played a pretty good straight trombone. He wasn't going to get off man, you know. But he played the notes right.
Did you stick mostly to the sax then or did you switch your arms?

No, I switched when I'm playing clarinet. But no, you had to play sax in those days to stay with the band. All the range, you had to play exactly what was written. Only when you take it solo that you play with your field and the band.
Yeah, you know, you play a large solo. Yeah.
How many arrangers did Louis Armstrong have with him?

Well, we used to get our two numbers a week. We got from different arrangers. We had different numbers, but they knew Louis' style. We had one guy in New York just arranged for us. Let's see, I forgot his name though. Very good arranger. Oh, I can't call his name now. Oh, we had different guys. Every week we could get two new numbers and we'd run them down.
But in the band, did anybody arrange?

Yeah, Louis Russell. George Washington, Louis Russell, and Bingham Addison. Bingham Addison on the end. He was a good arranger also. Bingham could arrange without a piano just by his ear. Very good musician. He's a stunning arranging.
Were your arrangements easy to play?

Well, you'd get used to them, yeah. You'd get used to them, sure. We'd take, when we came off the road from the least one night, as we'd go on the road saying, Joe Green would build a tune for us for two months. The Easton tune, the Western tune, and the Southern tune, and all that sort of stuff. When we'd come back, we'd buy new arrangements, different tunes. Now, we'd take a number. The reeds would get into this side of the hall, or wherever we were rehearsing. The brass gets over, the trombones get over there, the trumpet's over here, and the rhythm section stays with the piano. And we'd just run over to get the notes together. Then when we got it, in about a half an hour, we'd say, all right, you fellas ready, you're here. But then we'd go up, we'd play it for the sound, to see what's happening. We'd play the tune that's written. Then the ideas start coming, and the pops would say, well, the second chorus, Nick, you'd take the first 16 balls, or the middle of the chorus, or whatever it is. And I'd check it off. And then when the trombone, Hickey, take that, and Charlie Holmes, you'd take this, and Red Allen, you'd take this, and pops would take the rest. And then, we'd run over it like that. Then when we'd get it down, two or three times, we'd put that number aside, we'd take the album. We'd just rehearse two numbers. And at night, when we'd playin' on the job, in the first set, we'd put one of those numbers in the set, in the middle part some way. And before we'd close, we'd play it again. And after we didn't eat the music, we'd memorize, we'd show up on memorizing. That's the main thing. Louie is the greatest musician I know for memorizing. He was fantastic. This man would take a tune he'd never seen before. He'd stick his handkerchief in his trumpet, and he's concentrating on the notes. And when he'd say, all right, pops, we're ready, you're it. He'd go up there, and he might put the part up at rehearsal. At night, memorizing, you know, just that quick.
You think he was the man that we'd do? What Lewis could read, man. Don't let nobody kid you.

Yes, he had to be, to play with all those bands in three years. A lot of people believe that Lewis was from Orleans, an old-timer. They had such a stupid question. They said, do Lewis read? Does he read? He played Fletcher's book, first, second, and third book, because when Lewis read Fletcher, he made the band. If you get those old records with Lewis. These other guys, Lewis didn't drink at the time. They'd get drunk sometimes, and you know, Lewis would play first, second, and third. Man, Lewis was a great musician. He's the greatest of all of them. I don't give a darn who you mentioned. Pops was because. And what a memory this man had. Because you had these arrangements sometime in unison, four trumpets. And these guys, they're looking at their pups. Pops is out there, standing out there, don't miss a note. And you hear him above them. They sound like little boys when Lewis is playing. I'm telling you, no, no. This is something else.
To get back to the early days, did you watch the other clarinet players carefully? Did you watch them to figure out anything?

Yes, you sure you got ears. I tell you, when I was coming up, I admired Artie Shaw was my favorite clarinet player. Benny Goodman, he played nice, but he was a mechanical to me. I didn't copy him, but I knew what they were making. But Artie Shaw had something else. He had a beautiful sound. He was a great musician. And this man was something else. I liked his band, Artie Shaw, in the third. You had another one you had. You had a lot of clarinet players. But it was all imitating Benny. And that was a little, Benny had got a strong tone and was a good musician. I'm not putting that now. But it isn't for me to imitate. It's mechanical. It's something. Now, I like Edmund Hall. He's got soul. Benny ain't got no soul. He play technical, he runs over, beautiful. But Hall had something, he had guts. And who else? Pee Wee Russell. He had guts. He had something else. A little something different, you know, in the clarinet. Oh, he had many of them. Jimmy D'Arcy, he was a good tune. Jimmy D'Arcy. He had his stuff going also. Who else had? Uh, Bonnie B. Dodd came when he went with Duke. Bonnie had something. Bonnie was playing some beautiful clarinet with Duke. Did he play clarinet down here in New Orleans? No. He didn't. He, when I left to go to China in 1924, 1926 rather. Bonnie took my place and he improved on these. And when he went with Duke, I was surprised when I came back, you know, two or three years away. One time, we were at the Saratoga Club, and we were working the whole year round, not even one night off in the whole year. So we told Russell, we said, man, we're tired. We're going to leave there. We're going to the Roseland Ballroom two months back to Saratoga. Tour, make theater, Lowest State and all those places, go to Washington, D.C., come back. So finally we took two weeks off. Russell put another band in the Saratoga, and said, well, these fellas have two weeks. And Jelly was there that night. He heard about it. He said, Russell, I want to use your band. I said, it's okay, because next week we'll be off two weeks. And then he started sending these Steelers out, you know, for two of them. He said, Russell, I'm going to give you $50 a night to stay home. That's right. Now this is funny. I'm going to give you $50 a night to stay home. I don't need you. But your band. Took the whole band in tight. He didn't tell us how much he was going to pay us yet. But he told Russell, I remember that. Bob Foster, Red Island, Otis Johnson, Agen Bollett, we had one trombone at the time. Three Reeds, Greeley Walton, myself, and Charlie Holmes. And we had a solid match. Took our arrangements and took his arrangements. He had some good arrangements, too. So we rehearsed his arrangements in the daytime privately. We didn't let nobody know that he's taking our band. He's got, the first game we played was in Wilts Bay, Pennsylvania. Jelly went out and rented some Cadillacs. He rented about three times. He rented about three times. He rented about three times. He rented about three times. Second-hand, you know. And I drove one up myself. That's right. I drove one with about four to five guys in the band. And Red wasn't driving there. And we went in style. When we get to Wilts Bay, Pennsylvania, Jelly had played there before with a bad band. It didn't have no people in the place, you know. And the guy who was kind of salsa dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear And the guy was kind of strong, he said, well, Jelly, Jelly said, man, I got a band tonight. The man said, oh, Jelly, don't give me that stuff, man. You brought me a band last year. Jelly said, but now, tonight, man, I'm going to pack your place. He had two gigs there, you know, two nights. He said, tomorrow night the police will have to keep the people in line.
The man said, oh, Jelly, come on, come on.

If I have 150 people, I'll make it. And the police hold about 500. This was in a big park. And they had no broadcasting. The cats would come in the head of you by the window, see what kind of band you got. And if it was a good band, they'd tell us, and they'd come in. If it was a bad band, nobody happened.
Jelly said, oh, man, tonight I'm back to the place.
So, tomorrow night you'll get a compliment.
All right, Jelly.

So the man hadn't heard the band. You know, you just tell them. Nine o'clock, we hit. Everybody's in show uniform, short. Plenty of people out. Nobody come in. Nobody come. They're waiting to hear. Yeah. And so Jelly said, listen, don't tell them what band is. You know, just anybody ask you what band is. My band, you know. Don't see no Lloyd Russell or nothing like that. You know, it's probably. He said, yeah, okay, he got you covered. Man, we hit band. Jelly was directing. We played our arrangement. You know, first set, first three, four numbers of Jelly. Man, we hit, I was moving, Lloyd Russell. I said, wait a minute. Jelly's got a band. Then the word got around. They started buying tickets. And a half an hour, the place is almost full. Word, word to my, they're calling their friends. Here, Jelly's got a band, baby. Come on, here it is. Then Jelly, in the mission, at 10 o'clock, everybody said, Jesus Christ, where are you fellas from?
So, New York. Is this Jelly's band? Yeah.

You know, we didn't say we're the professors. Man, it's kind of bad. Oh, man. And Jelly was proud. He walked up to the bar. He said, you happy? The boss, he said, man, I didn't expect this. See, I told you, man. But tomorrow night, the cops will have to keep the people away. They're lying, you know. And he said, you sort of believe. He said, well, but Jelly, what band is this? Never mind, this is my band, man. And, man, we packed them in at night. The next night, before we hit at nine, the place is full. It was empty when we started the night before, you know. Nobody. It was full. When we got through playing the first number, there was a line outside. And the police was there telling the people, no more care. You see what I told you, man? Man, I'm Jelly Roe Morton. You see what I told you? And it was the truth. The man then he wanted. Another day, he wanted to hire, you know. Jelly said, no, man, I'm booked out. You see, because he got, you know. The man said, all right. I know you got, Jelly said, I go to so-and-so tomorrow. After this, I go to so-and-so. I go to so-and-so. The man said, well, when you finish, at the end of your tour, maybe in one month. Come on back. Jelly said, I'm booked out for a whole year.
I'm sorry.

I said, Jelly's funny. I'm booked out for a whole year. The man, man, is it money? No, man, I'm booked out. I can't. I'm booked out, man, for the whole year. You see, he never told a man it wasn't his man. And we had a successful tour. We come on back, and he paid us all very good. I think he gave us about $40 a night apiece, you know. That was good money in those days, you know, in 1933, 1932, like that. And man, and he paid Russell to stay at home, like he said. He paid Russell to go. And Jelly was happy. He came on back with the cars and everything. Jelly said, man.
He told Russell. He said, Russell, you've got a great band, but you don't know what to do with it.

You don't know what to do with it. And, you know. And Russell just laughed and said, man, man. I like Jelly. Jelly was great. He never, he never tinses out of one penny. We never asked him how much. We always were surprised. Jelly was something like that.
What year was that?
Around the, no, that was around 35, I think, 36. Yeah, I'm 36. That's before.
After that, General Wotter got into trouble.

Then he started getting in trouble. No, he had his brain then. Then it started tightening up on his, on his. Melrose was getting his brain. And he had his chute coming in. Oh, he was, he was heartbroken.
I didn't, I missed the part about the drinking with Jelly Roll.
I never saw him drink. Now, that's the said, when he made that album for Lomax, that he drank. I don't, never seen Jelly drink. One drop of liquor in it. And I never seen him smoke a cigarette.
Isn't that a picture of him smoking a cigarette, too?
Never seen him smoke.
I never, I don't remember that.
He may have. Or maybe he picked up drinking in his latest years. It's possible.
It's possible after, after I left, I went to California, actually. No, I was there. No, Jelly died. I don't think the country, I don't think.
You made a record with him pretty late, too, didn't you? I knew, well, yeah, I thought it. He didn't drink then, did you?
No, I never seen Jelly drink then. Well, what about the guys in the band? They did, right.
But Jelly said, I don't want nobody to get drunk. I hope you get drunk in my band.
You wouldn't let him drink as long as he didn't get drunk.

Yeah, he didn't. He didn't get drunk. He was, to me, he was one of the greatest. Jelly was one of the greatest. He would talk plenty, but he could back it up. You never could hem him up. I've never seen him lose an argument. When Jelly tells you something, you put your money on it, because he knows, he's got all the fundamental parts in front. He knew what he was talking about. And he was, after he died, all of you would say, man, that man was great. I'd say, yeah, but when he was living, you know, he talks plenty, blah, blah, blah. But Jelly was great, man.
Jelly was great. How did somebody like Chick Webb compare?

Chick had a good name. Chick had a good band. I worked with Chick about seven or eight months. I got Ty playing the same, the arrangements were rustling, you know. And I changed up, I went with Chick, and I came with Lloyd, came in the band, and Lloyd said, oh, man, come on back to the band. And so I just, we didn't fuss or nothing. I just got Ty playing the same music. Then I came on back and Lloyd wrestling again.
I was like, I think, 30, uh, 24, 35. Was Ward Pinkett any good then?
Ward was very good.
Ward was good. See, I never heard him much except with Jelly and one Joe Steele record.

Did you hear the record I made? Well, damn, I had a little band at the, after I left Chick a month later, I went, Agents Tappen, wait, you remember me? Yeah, yeah, I have heard of that. And I recorded with the band down there, and that was in the 36th. In 36th, that's what Louie had told me, oh, man, it's a little funny band, why don't you come on back in the band? Louie came from Chicago to make a tube with the band.
Mm-hmm.
And all the fans, of course, know why they couldn't play him. So, and the rest would say, oh, come on, man, stop all this. And I said, okay. And I came back in the band, stayed in 1940. Yeah.
Didn't they have any good clarinet players around New York, Michael?

They were, they were, they were play parts. They were pretty sad, but you had no one, no soul. You know, Barnaby Gardner and I, I think the two, two best ones around New York at the time. Yeah, I don't tell you.
Was Edmund Hall playing well then?

Edmund Hall was, and then he was playing, yeah, Edmund Hall was playing saxophone with, Claude Hopkins. Then he started getting on clarinet, you know what I mean? Mm-hmm. He wasn't known as a clarinet until after later on through the years. He didn't have any kind of like clarinet. Yeah.
And what about Alex Hill? Was his band better? No, that was just a recording. He never had a band. Yeah, he was a recording. I'm trying to think of this arranger.
He was a very good arranger for that power band. The Louis Russell's band.
He had Bingham Madison, this arranger, Louis Russell, and George Washington.

He had four arrangers in the band. Plus this cat used to arrange for us. He was very good. He was very good. With which band? The Louis Russell's band. He had Bingham Madison, this arranger, Louis Russell, and George Washington. There was four arrangers in the band. Plus this cat used to arrange for us. He knew the style of the band. Did you ever know a guy named Chappy Willard? Chappy Willard, that's him. How old was he? Chappy Willard? Chappy Willard, that's him. Chappy Willard was an arranger. He was a very good. He was a very good. With which band? The Louis Russell's band. With which band? The Louis Russell's band. They had Bingham Madison, this arranger, Louis Russell, and George Washington. There were four arrangers in the band. Plus this cat used to arrange for us. He knew the style of the band. Did you ever know a guy named Chappy Willard? Chappy Willard, that's him. Chappy Willard was an arranger.
He didn't band anything, he has the arranger. He was a right.
Hell of a arranger.
How did you get it?
Well, through the years, he was a great guy.
He was a great guy. He was a great guy. How did you get it? How did you get it?
Well, through the years, you know what I mean, when everything was happening. He started arranging two numbers first a week, and he knew the band's sound.
He was very good.
Chappy Willard, I was trying to think of him.
I never have known anything about him, where he was from. I just said his name. Pennsylvania. He was a musician. What did he play?
I don't know what he played. I never heard him play.
He played a big show. He played a big show.
He played a big show. He played a big show.
Well, Paul Barberin used to tell me that Joe Glazer had some white arrangers.
He had some white arrangers also. I'm forgetting the name. No.
Joe Glazer took the band over.
That's when Russell lost the band. Joe Glazer took over. I guess he made big money. He did.
He made millions for Joe. We knew he made millions for Joe Glazer.

When Joe Glazer came with Louis, he was a big show. He had nothing. Louis just had the trumpet. Joe Glazer had that one suit. I remember that. He was hustling. He started booking the band. He had a little piece. Mills had an office. Joe Glazer had a little corner where he used to get the ring. The next year, Joe Glazer had an office in Radio City. One office. The following year, he had the whole floor. Then he was. Everybody singing. Mills had an office. Joe Grady had a little corner where he used to get the radio. The next year, Joe Grady had an office in Radio City, one office. The following year, he had the whole floor. Then he had other, Hollywood was working for him. That man knows his music. Then he was, everybody, singers, he had them under his fingertips, you know, the percentage. Dancers under Joe Nathan. He had Enterprise. Then he was a millionaire. He was a multimillionaire when he died. Did you make any movies, by the way? We made one in New York. That was with a singer, Martin Donnelly. You know Martin Donnelly? I know who you're talking about. In fact, that was something I can just talk about. He had a very nice tenor voice, Irishman. We made this in New York. This was around 1934 or 1933 in Long Island. It was a deal of the movie. It was a lot of plot to the picture. I saw the picture after. We had a little point in it. It was like a music store. Russell comes in. He's a talkie. He said, Hey, that's where it's Russell. Why don't you join us and do something. He said, Mr. Donnelly is here. Why don't you play it now? We played one number for him. He said, we played one bounce and that was all. And so Russell said, yes. And then we got, he said, you got your instruments? He said, yes. And so we all come on. This was street clothes, no? Like the old music show. They came on in and we, and walked down. I forgot what he sang. It's a long time ago. One number, he was back. And he showed that. Danny said, come on and play us something for dancing. And he played this tune for our own arrangement of this, and that was this foul part. And then the rest of the picture had a little bit of a play. I saw it at the Radio City. I saw a little short movie one time with
the Armstrong and the new Russell band. I wonder if you were in there. It was one of those little
short ones. He just went on tune. Yeah, that's it. I think. No, Louie wasn't on that. Oh yeah.
Now this is sing, this is must be made later. Later, later, later. Yeah, yeah. Well, they made a lot of little one-wheel. I remember that you were in there. Yeah, yeah.

I mean, there was. I don't know, but I don't remember this one. Now, when I was with the big man in California, we played at Sam Sebastian's Cotton Club. They had two reviews, the color review and the white review for two months. Louie was in the phone, man. We recorded that. The skeleton in the closet. Yeah. And all that. And that's Shabby Willis-Ranger. She's got the closet. What the hell was a random. And we did a recording date there. For Decca, I think, or Columbia. It must have been Decca. Decca. And that was a hell of a van we had.
That's a number that Lee Collins played when he came up to your club on the excursion. Remember? Mm-hmm. The saxophone player was telling us about Lee coming up there and playing that number.

Mm-hmm. I tell you, we sent him and got Lee when Red Allen came in the band, and Otis Jones. We were on two trumpets, you see. And we sent him and we got Lee. And Lee was, he could play good, but he couldn't read. And you had to read because the numbers were tight, you know. But for solos, Lee, yeah, he played. He played beautiful trumpet. But he couldn't read enough to stay with it. He stayed with us about three or four, about a month. He tried to break it. I mean, show him the parts, but he just didn't learn to read. Yeah. He probably didn't have the training. He didn't have the training for the band, but we gave him some work to do. We played around him and let him go, you know, let him play. But to get back with the band, you know, it's even. He had to let him go. And he couldn't make it. He couldn't make it. He couldn't make it. So he went on back. He went back to New Orleans? He went back to New Orleans. This was in the 30s. Yeah. Lee was a strong niche. Good guy, dude. He couldn't make it.
What about Otis Johnson? What did he play? Third? He played third.

Played third. He didn't do any solo work. No, no. He rented the solo work. And Bill Dillard, he was our first trumpet player at the time, early part. Then Hemphill, when Louie, Hemphill, Duke Ellington, he came with us. He's a fine first trumpet player. Very good. Read all the other. See, we had two bands. We had two sets of music. One with Louie and one with our band. In the Mission, when Pop takes off In the Mission, then we go with Red Allen. Listen at this one. That's where Red would get off, you know. And the people said, gee, listen at that band. Then we go back to Louie again. He'd play Louie's two of them.
A very interesting band. Would Louie mostly play the same program?
Oh, yeah. We'd play, you see. We had a book for Louie and a book for our band. We had two books for our band. We had three books of music, all arranged. I noticed that in the lady, yes,
Louie would always play the same program, always every night like that. Well, yes.

Most of them like that in those days too? Yes, he'd play mostly the same thing. Because you see, on a tour, you don't break up your... We had about five sets of night, eight numbers, that's 40 numbers a night. Well, sometimes we mix, we do a mixture of things. We don't request, we pay anything you want. But we get outstanding things.
What about if people would ask you that you didn't have a race before you played anyway?

Well, they have a few things you'd ask for that we didn't have. We had really everything in the album. Russ, we had it from Red Allen or we had it from Pops. You had to read a big book. Yeah, he had a hell of a book. Russ had music, no. You didn't play many heads at all? No, we didn't. We had played most arrangements. I'll tell you one time, yeah, we were in Chicago at the Grand Terrace for two weeks. Fox had the job. And I remember, Joe Clayton's buddy. And you remember? My name is the shame. They had an arguing in the band. Somebody said, but I don't like this tune. I don't like that tune. And I remember at the rehearsal, Lewis said, Pops said, man, let me tell you, there's no bad tunes. All tunes are good. What do you mean, Pops? It's the way you play them. There's no bad tunes, I tell you. The guy said, yeah, no bad tunes. He said, there's no bad, and I noticed one thing, everything he made was a hit. And he's right, there's no bad tune. So, me and Mr. Shen had just come out, that she called them. And during the animation, the band was off to stand. And just Louie, Pop, and Paul Barberin, and Pop Foster, and Lee Blair, stayed on the stand. And Pops, Joe Russell, played with me and Mr. Shen. Just by himself. And Louie played such a beautiful horn. I never heard, he's always playing arrangements, you know. Now he's at live. Pops started blowing, and the people started, what? They went crazy. And Pops took about eight chorus of Lumi and the band. And they said, man, now we had to keep that number in for two weeks because they thought it was in the act. They thought it was in the act, you know. Hey, that number of the Pops, they ain't playing the band no mine. They want to hear Louie. And Louie said, you see what I tell you? There's no bad tune. Now we were convinced, you know. Now that we, I knew it all. Come on. Lord, Louie shook him. Louie's in good form. Oh, man. That was the time when Joe Louie was champion, and he was there with his wife that night. He just played. That place was packed. And every night, Louie had to do Louie. That Mr. Shen business.
Oh, that was funny. He could make the people like anything, did he?

I'm telling you, I never heard of him sound bad through the ears. Anything he played, it was in that song. Oh, Lord, Lord. Well, he was right. That's the way you played. Hey, cats, I don't like this number. I don't know why. I don't like it. Oh, come on.
Oh, what was the Maple Leaf band? We mentioned that.

That was the first band I played with. That was with old time. That's with old Gaspar on bass. And his brother Vic on trombone. There was a whole bunch of, I forgot the band for so long. It was around 1950. When I first started playing in 1950. Was it a tunk band? No, no, it was just a, yeah, they were in music at the time. Yeah, yeah, yeah. What kind of music did you use? Well, we used stock arrangements. Just simple tunes. Because it was popular we played. We played with what was happening at the time.
Little pop tunes. Just playing them naturally. Did you play any of the Red Book stuff then?
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. I forgot about that book. Scott, that thing from St. Louis. They had a Red Book and they had a Green Book, didn't they? They had two.
Well, my teacher used to say the Green Book was the one that you played by ear. But I don't know. I don't know, man. They had some of them.

That's how I knew Louis could read. You know, he's talking about reading. When Louis was on the boat with Faith Marvel. And Louis was on the boat for about three or four years. Faith Marvel and then taught Louis to read. I was amazed when Louis came off that boat. He came around and taught him, and he was playing with us. We got in that Red Book, man. And didn't miss a note. That's a tough book. Yeah, man.
And you knew him before? Faith was the one who taught him?
Faith taught him. Faith taught him. And you knew him before, though? Oh, I knew him. And he went back to June when he was a kid.
And he was not a good player.

Well, he started with a bugle and then he started with trumpet. And when he came out, he couldn't read nothing. He went on the boat with Faith and stayed about three or four years. When he come off that boat, he was reading his ass off. He was reading then. He was reading ever since. And he made a record. One of his best records was in Hollywood with this symphony band in New York. This great conductor you have. Bernstein. Did you hear that record?
It wasn't supposed to be.
Oh, man. I got it at home.
It's almost all on there, I think.

St. Louis Blues. They got a big symphonic arrangement with all those strings and trumpets. And pops came on there like a champ. Different movements. That man played. And when they got through with it, this man's dedicated. He said, ladies and gentlemen, he said, we just heard, he says, Lewis always said that he wanted to play with the symphony. He says, we are honored to have this man with us because he's such an artist that when he's practicing, when he makes one note, he's such an inspiration, which it is. Pop just can, when he's tuned up, just went boom. That's the man right there. It's different from any sound you ever heard in the trumpet. I knew he was something else, man. He said, then we are honored. See, this man is not only great, he's, he's, he's, oh, he's getting a good thing off on this record. He's something else. And pops couldn't say nothing. He was chalked up. And so, you know, I said, well, ladies and gentlemen, I want to thank you. This is my first time playing in the symphony. I just don't know what to say, folks. He was chalked up, but that was a bad, I got the record on. Oh, man. And Handy was in the place with it. That man arranged with the symphonic parade in St. Louis Blues. And Pops come on in there like a champ. Oh, my, that was years ago, in Hollywood Bowl. How was Johnny Dawson's, uh, the reader? I don't know. You see, I never played with Johnny. He was with King Arthur. He, I think he could, Marshall could read a little bit, yeah. I don't know who he took lessons with.
He never did play with Marshall reading bands, did he? No, no, no. You see, he never played sax. He never

played with no bands. I see, yeah. Just in Orleans. Did you know Jimmy Noon down there? Oh, yes. I knew Jimmy Noon as a kid. He took, Jimmy Noon was a hell of a musician. He was high, man. Beautiful, man. He played with Charlie Cook's band. He played with Chicago. He played with Chicago. He threw it sound and oh, he played. He seemed to be very fast.
He wasn't yet. He had a little teenage. Yeah. He took every note. Yeah, he was fast.

He used to try to steal from Jimmy. Bonnie and I were coming up. I used to like Jimmy's band. Especially at Chikong, we were at this place, then, after our place. Forget the name of his club. Apex. Apex. Jimmy Alquantete. Oh, man. All the musicians, they would come there packing up and like this.
He played sax too, didn't you? No, he didn't buy sax. He stayed up with him. He had a big band in later years. Yeah, I know. Before he died. Yeah.
Just when he was making it again, he died. Did you ever have any battles of music like with Charlie Cook or anybody like that? No, in Chicago, you never had. You see,

you know, I remember those days. Kid Renee, oh, that's a little good sort of plays then. Kid Renee, he was there too. Chalky Banana. Dead. Oh, these wagons, you know. You know, in the corner there, I saw these balls like on a Sunday night, Sunday afternoon, going different neighborhoods and they battle. These were hellfire days in the morning. That was the second line, following the band all over the street. Did you play parade yourself? Yes. I played one or two before I went to the hood. But who? Manny Parism, all my friends. Oh, you were?
Yeah. OBB, huh? Did you play the E flat then? Yes. I learned on the E flat when I was a kid. My fingers

wasn't big enough to stretch to me. Oh, you started. I learned the hardest one first. Then I led on a chance. You started out on the album system. I started on the album system. My home broke down. I was in the old E.J. in 1927, 1928. I had to send it to Paris to get fixed. And this man, a classical man, in the hotel, you see, and he said, why don't you play the poem? I said, oh, no, man. He said, that's a better issue for you. I hear you playing with. And he said, it's too hard. He said, it's easier. I'll teach it. And he normally barely get going, you see. And he said, well, you have to practice at least two hours at the end. We can go there. I said, okay. I took the horn. And he showed them the same way. It's still different in the same way. Showed me the correct way. And I practiced at the back of two weeks. Then I got it. And about a month later, they sent my horn from the rest to me. I forgot all my album system. I had forgotten it. So I got it. I got it. I got it. I like it. I like it. So that's why I bought it all. They figured it. It doesn't change. It doesn't change. It doesn't change. It doesn't change. It doesn't change. I didn't ask if we could have a massive of this game.
Well, nobody could do any faster than me now. I don't know.
Well, I don't think he was done with this.
Oh, no.
I'm not a moniker. I'm not a musician.
Oh, shit. I'm a musician. You don't have much anymore.
I don't have a time. Do you have time to do another? No, I think there's one. Oh.
But I know.
Yeah, we do. And we've got plenty. We've got very good.
